Prove that after r stages the resulting permutation p agrees with e on every original index, i.e. p(castLE a) = e(a) for all a < r.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Reorienting an orthogonal matrix to determinant 1 by a single sign-flip chosen from column-permutation parity yields an orthogonal det-1 matrix on both parity branches, without ever evaluating the determinant.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: An orthogonal matrix U is reoriented to have determinant 1 by multiplying it with a sign-flip on a single designated unused column exactly when U already has the wrong sign; the choice is made by the parity (sign) of an accompanying column permutation, not by evaluating the determinant. Prove the reoriented matrix is orthogonal with determinant 1 regardless of which branch is taken.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Symmetric Gray-coordinate relabeling of a matrix preserves orthogonality and the determinant exactly, because one shared row/column bijection makes it a multiplicative identity-fixing reindexing.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: A real matrix indexed by width-(q+1) computational-basis labels is converted to Gray coordinates by relabeling both its rows and its columns through a fixed bijection between labels and the numerical indices 0..2^(q+1)-1 (the same bijection on each side). Prove that this relabeling preserves orthogonality, i.e. if A^T A = I then the Gray-coordinate matrix is again orthogonal, and that it preserves the determinant exactly. Identify precisely why using the same bijection on rows and columns is essential.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Reindexing an adjacent plane rotation by the Gray labeling equals a selected RY two-level plane on the Gray-flip wire; the half-angle is theta or -theta according to the first index's target bit, from the pair ordering.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: A real SO matrix on 2^(q+1) Gray-ordered indices is compiled to a circuit by first decomposing it into adjacent plane rotations, then realizing each plane as a selected RY rotation whose target wire is the single Gray-flip wire of that adjacent pair, with every other wire a control. Prove that reindexing the adjacent plane matrix by the Gray labeling equals the selected two-level plane on that target wire, and explain how the half-angle sign depends on the target bit of the first index.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Two basis states share a selected RY plane's control context if and only if they are equal or related by a single target-wire X, pinning the exact 2D pair the rotation can touch.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: A selected RY plane fixes every computational-basis vector whose control context differs from the chosen one, and acts as a 2x2 real rotation on the single pair sharing the chosen context and differing on the target bit. Prove that two basis states lie in the same control context if and only if they are equal or related by a single X action on the target wire.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: The unoptimized Gray/Givens producer emits L=N(N-1)/2 selected planes, each3*2^q-2 gates. Its exact family ratio G/N grows quadratically, while the N4 check only distinguishes stage cost from total cost; none is an optimal-synthesis lower bound.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: A selected RY rotation with c controls uses exactly 2^c RY gates and 2*(2^c - 1) CX gates per selected rotation and makes zero oracle calls. A reader claims that because a general real SO matrix on these wires is realized by such selected planes, the per-stage gate counts show the SO matrix is prepared in a number of gates linear in the matrix dimension. Give a boundary/counterexample analysis of why that linear-in-dimension conclusion does not follow from the per-rotation counts.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Iterated step-by-step application of a plane-rotation list equals one multiplication by the accumulated matrix taken in reverse list order; the reverse order is forced by first-listed-acts-first.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: A list of plane rotations can be applied to a matrix in two ways. The step-by-step action takes the list and the matrix and applies the first listed rotation to the matrix, then the next to the result, and so on. Alternatively one forms a single accumulated matrix from the list (built so that the last listed rotation multiplies on the left-most, i.e. the product is taken in reverse-list order) and multiplies it once against the matrix. Prove that these two procedures agree for every list and every matrix, and explain why the accumulated product must be taken in reverse list order.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: In an eight-counter exact-real operation model, prove a stored two-row plane rotation on length-M rows costs exactly 6*M field, 10*M read and 6*M write operations, accounting for each from the three materialized passes.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: Work in an exact-real word-operation model that keeps eight separate running counters: field operations, square roots, inverse-cosine calls, other trigonometric calls, exact comparisons, stored-word reads, stored-word writes, and emitted records. Each primitive call adds one unit to its own counter; proof checking, counter bookkeeping and loop-index arithmetic are free, and stored data are nested vectors. A plane rotation acts on two stored length-M real rows u and v with coefficients c and s, returning rows whose j-th entries are c*u_j - s*v_j and s*u_j + c*v_j. The implementation first materializes a stored vector of M computed entry-pairs, then materializes the first output row and the second output row as two further stored passes. Every materialized pass over M indices additionally charges two reads and two writes per index to write each intermediate value and read it back for projection, and each single entry-pair is computed with exactly the six field operations c*u_j, s*v_j, s*u_j, c*v_j, their difference, and their sum. Prove that rotating the two rows costs exactly 6*M field operations, 10*M reads and 6*M writes, and account for the origin of every read and write.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Prove one stored rotation step costs 6*M field, 10*M+2*N+2 read and 6*M+2*N write operations, where the 2*N spine-copy term is a stipulated charge of the cost contract.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: Continue in the eight-counter exact-real operation model where stored matrices are vectors of N stored rows and replacing one stored row is charged as a full persistent copy costing N reads and N writes, never an in-place update. A rotation step on an N-by-M stored matrix reads the two rows i and j to be combined, computes the two rotated rows (whose production costs 6*M field, 10*M read and 6*M write), and then stores the two new rows with two separate persistent row-replacements. Prove that one such rotation step costs 6*M field operations, 10*M + 2*N + 2 reads, and 6*M + 2*N writes, and explain why the step cannot be made cheaper by assuming in-place row updates.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: By induction on step count, prove a k-step column sweep is bounded by k*(step budget + emit) on every counter and emits exactly k records including zero-angle steps.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: In the eight-counter exact-real model, a column sweep eliminates entries below a pivot by performing a chronological chain of elimination steps. Each step first computes an elimination angle and the two rotation coefficients (bounded by a fixed per-step budget B that is independent of which branch of the angle computation is taken), applies a rotation to the stored matrix, and then emits exactly one rotation record (one unit on the emitted-record counter). A sweep performing k steps is defined by recursion: zero steps emit nothing and do no work; a sweep of k+1 steps performs one elimination step and then recurses on the resulting matrix, emitting one record for the step. Prove by induction on k that (a) the total cost of a k-step sweep is at most k*(B + one emit) on every counter, and (b) the emitted-record counter equals exactly k, even though some steps may rotate by a harmless zero angle.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: By list induction, prove a stored replay of L recorded rotations denotes the product of plane rotations (not formed densely) and costs L times a per-step budget plus one trailing read.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: A rectangular elimination records a chronological list of two-row rotation steps. Rather than forming the accumulated orthogonal transform by multiplying out dense plane-rotation matrices, a stored replay starts from a materialized identity and re-applies each recorded two-row rotation to the stored matrix in order; the empty list charges one read of the end marker, and each recorded step charges one read of the record, one field operation for halving its angle, two trigonometric calls for the pair of coefficients, and one stored two-row rotation. On a k-by-N working matrix a single such rotation costs the fixed amount described earlier (field, read and write terms linear in N and in the matrix dimension). Prove two things about replaying a list of L steps: first, that the result denotes exactly the product of the recorded plane rotations applied to the starting matrix, and second, that the total cost is L times a fixed per-step budget plus one extra read, with the extra read coming from the empty-list base case.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Prove the eight per-counter polynomial budgets of a stored rectangular compilation sum to N*M*(22*M+30*N+29)+5*N*N+4*N+M+1 and read it as an exact-real, not finite-bit, count. The write budget includes the required +2*N spine term.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: A full stored rectangular compilation of an N-by-M matrix produces a reduced residual, a chronological list of rotation steps, and a fully accumulated N-by-N transform. In the eight-counter exact-real model its per-counter cost has been bounded by an explicit polynomial budget whose values on the eight counters are: field = N*M*(6*M+6*N+9); square root = N*M; inverse-cosine = N*M; other trigonometric = 4*N*M; comparison = 2*N*M + M + N*N; read = N*M*(10*M+14*N+10) + 2*N*N + 2*N + 1; write = N*M*(6*M+10*N+1) + 2*N*N + 2*N; emitted records = N*M. Prove that the sum of all eight counters is bounded by N*M*(22*M+30*N+29) + 5*N*N + 4*N + M + 1, and explain why this single scalar is an operation count in an extended exact-real model and not a finite-bit running time.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: A wide thin-LQ run has an exact sum of actual stage costs, but only an upper bound after the compiler cost is replaced by its polynomial budget; its deterministic factors satisfy the exact same-run LQ identities.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question:
Let A be a stored real m-by-n matrix, with m at most n. Its wide thin-LQ routine transposes A, runs the full stored rectangular compiler on the transpose, extracts R as an m-by-m matrix from the residual, and extracts Q as an m-by-n matrix from the accumulated transform. Costs are vectors of nonnegative integer operation counters. Write C(X) for the actual counter vector of the rectangular compiler on stored input X, and P(N,M) for its declared polynomial upper budget, so C(X) is at most P(N,M) componentwise for every N-by-M X. For an N-by-M materialization whose entries each read one row and one entry, the exact counter vector is E(N,M)=2*N*M*tick(read)+(N*M+N)*(2*tick(read)+2*tick(write)). Here tick(op) is one unit in counter op and zero in the others. Let At be the actual stored transpose produced by the first stage.

Assess the assertion that the actual wide cost always equals E(n,m)+P(n,m)+E(m,m)+E(m,n). Give a concrete counterexample if it is false; the emit counter at m=n=1 is a useful discriminator. Then derive the exact additive identity in terms of C(At), and prove the resulting componentwise upper bound. Finally show that the R and Q returned by this same routine satisfy A=R*Q and Q*Q-transpose=I_m, including rank-deficient inputs and empty dimensions. Distinguish this wide routine from the all-shape dispatcher and keep operation counts separate from finite-bit runtime.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Prove a size-k monadic sum of equal-cost summands costs k*(B+one field), and specialize to a bond-D contraction entry costing D*(three reads + two field).
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: In the eight-counter exact-real model, a bounded sum over an index set of size k is evaluated by a monadic fold: starting from the pure value zero (no charge), each of the k summands is produced and then added to the running accumulator with one field addition. Suppose every summand has the same per-counter cost B. Prove that the whole sum costs exactly k*(B + one field operation). Then specialize to a single contraction entry over a bond of size D, where each summand reads one entry of a stored core (two reads) and one entry of a stored vector (one read) and multiplies them (one field), so B is three reads plus one field, and conclude that the entry costs exactly D*(three reads + two field operations).

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Prove the stored chain closure costs 20*D-squared+30*D+5*n-squared+7*n+constant, explaining the n-squared term as a reference-copy series and the n-independent left closure.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: A stored matrix-product chain over n+1 cores, each of bond size D, is closed into a scalar-boundary chain in two conceptual halves. First the tail is processed recursively: at the last position the terminal core is contracted against a right boundary vector, and at every earlier position the current core is kept while the remaining table is copied by reference and the tail is recursed; a fixed small per-node record is charged at each position. Second the leftmost core is contracted against a left boundary vector. The returned chain exactly refines the kernel chain contracted against the two boundary vectors. Prove that the summed cost of the whole closure is bounded by a polynomial that is quadratic in the chain length n and cubic-free but quadratic in the bond D, and explain why the tail recursion contributes an n-squared term while the single left closure contributes only a bond-dependent term with no dependence on n.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: By chain induction, prove the stored Gram-environment computation costs at most n*(24*D-cubed+25*D-squared+20*D+6)+5*D-squared+4*D+6, with the cubic term from the per-node contractions.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: A stored tensor-train norm is computed by streaming local Gram environments from right to left. At the empty tail the environment is a materialized identity of bond size r. At a non-empty node carrying a core of left bond l and right bond m, the recursively computed right environment E (an m-by-m stored matrix) is updated: for each of the two physical bits the core slice is contracted with E (a first materialized pass) and the result is contracted with the transposed slice (a second materialized pass), and the two per-bit matrices are added; a fixed six-word node record is charged. Each per-node update therefore costs on the order of l*m*m + l*l*m matrix-contraction work plus additive and materialization terms. Assume every bond along a length-n chain is at most D. Prove by induction on the chain that the total summed cost of the Gram computation is bounded by n*(24*D-cubed + 25*D-squared + 20*D + 6) + 5*D-squared + 4*D + 6.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Prove the stored tensor-train norm costs the Gram cost plus exactly two reads and one square root (total +3), and equals the Euclidean norm of the represented vector.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: Given the stored right-to-left Gram-environment computation of a scalar-boundary tensor-train chain (which returns a 1-by-1 stored environment), the stored norm is obtained by reading the single scalar entry of that environment and taking its exact square root. Prove that the norm computation's cost equals the Gram computation's cost plus exactly two reads and one square root on the appropriate counters, and hence that its summed total exceeds the Gram total by exactly three. Then state precisely what mathematical quantity the returned scalar equals and why charging only two reads and one square root is the correct marginal cost of the scalar boundary.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Prove the sum-over-tags total equals the eight-term enumerated total, is additive, zero on the zero cost and one on a unit charge, and explain why this enables compositional cost proofs.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: Two notions of total cost appear in the stored exact-real model. One, call it the ordinary total, is the sum of a cost function over the finite type of all operation tags. The other, call it the enumerated total, is the explicit eight-term sum field + square root + inverse-cosine + other-trig + comparison + read + write + emitted-record. Prove that these two totals are equal as functions of the cost, that the total of a sum of two costs is the sum of their totals, that the total of the zero cost is zero, and that the total of a single unit charge on one tag is one. Explain why these simple algebraic facts are exactly what licenses replacing a sum-over-tags by the fixed eight-term expression in later cost proofs.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Prove the four named integer counters of the stored Hermite raw-source run sum to 2*n-squared+10*n+7, and delineate the same-run scope excluding finite-bit runtime and normalization.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: A stored Hermite raw-source assembly builds a scalar-boundary tensor-train chain for a state-preparation amplitude. One single run of the assembly returns the chain together with a work ledger carrying both the eight ordinary exact-real counters and four separately named integer counters (quotient calls, remainder calls, integer doublings, integer additions), plus a count of exponential-function calls. For parameters k and n it is proved on the same run that the chain denotes the explicit raw-source kernel chain, that the ordinary total is bounded by a stated polynomial in k and n, that the exponential calls are at most 3*(n+1)+1, and that the four integer counters equal (n+1)*(n+2), (n+1)-squared, n, and 4*(n+1) respectively. Prove that the four integer counters sum to 2*n-squared + 10*n + 7, and explain carefully which costs this certificate does and does not account for, especially regarding finite-bit arithmetic and normalization.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Prove a primitive circuit's parallel-scheduling depth is at most its gate count via the per-step inequality that one gate raises every wire depth by at most one.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: A primitive quantum circuit is a chronological list of gates, each gate acting on a set of touched wires. A per-wire scheduling fold tracks, for every wire, the earliest layer at which its next gate can be placed: processing a gate pushes every touched wire to one more than the maximum current depth over the gate's touched wires, and leaves untouched wires unchanged. The circuit depth is the maximum over all wires of the final per-wire depths; the gate count is the length of the list. Prove that the circuit depth is at most the gate count, i.e. that scheduling in parallel layers never makes the reported depth exceed the number of gates. Identify the key per-step inequality that drives the induction.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Materialization has no uniform dimensions-only cost bound over unrestricted suppliers: a fixed one-by-one zero matrix can be supplied with arbitrarily many charged additions. Polynomial bounds require control of the supplier work, not merely a storage surcharge.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: A stored N-by-M matrix is built by materializing an entry supplier: for each of the N*M entries the supplier is run to produce a value, and the construction charges, on top of the supplier's own counted work, two reads and two writes per entry plus two reads and two writes per row to store and project. The proved cost identity is that the materialized matrix costs the double sum of the supplier's per-entry costs plus (N*M + N) times the two-read-two-write surcharge. A colleague claims this identity proves that building any N-by-M stored matrix always costs a fixed polynomial in N and M alone. Give a precise counterexample showing the claim is false, and state the exact condition under which a clean polynomial-in-dimensions bound does hold.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: The angle budget is a componentwise upper bound. Zero inputs use no inverse cosine; nonzero inputs use one, but the full field budget is attained only when the negative-y sign branch executes its extra subtraction.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: The elimination-angle routine in the exact-real model computes a norm from two inputs x and y: it squares both, adds them, takes a square root, and tests whether that root is zero. If the root is zero it returns the angle zero immediately; otherwise it divides, takes an inverse cosine, tests the sign of y, conditionally negates, doubles, and negates again. A branch-independent angle budget of seven field operations, one square root, one inverse-cosine and two comparisons is proved to be an upper bound on the angle cost for all inputs. A colleague concludes that every call to the angle routine performs exactly one inverse-cosine call. Refute this with a specific input, and explain the precise logical relationship between the proved budget and the actual per-input cost.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Boundary: the stored identity costs 5*N*N+4*N exact-real operations, nonzero for all N at least 1, free only at the degenerate N=0.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: In the stored exact-real model the identity matrix of size N is not a primitive constant but is materialized: each of the N*N entries is produced by an exact comparison deciding whether its row and column indices are equal (returning one or zero), and the materialization adds the standard two-read-two-write surcharge per entry and per row. The proved identity cost is N*N comparisons plus (N*N + N) times the two-read-two-write surcharge. A colleague treats the stored identity as a zero-cost input when bounding a larger algorithm. Explain why this is wrong in general, work out the exact summed cost, and determine the boundary size N at which the identity genuinely costs nothing.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Counterexample: persistent log append costs the left length in reads and writes and is independent of the right length, so it is neither constant nor total-length dependent.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: When a stored sweep concatenates its chronological step logs, it uses a persistent list append that copies the spine of the left list while sharing the right list unchanged; the append is charged exactly the length of the left list in reads and the same in writes, with the right list contributing nothing. A colleague asserts two things: first that appending two logs is a constant-cost pointer operation, and second that the cost depends on the total number of records in both logs. Show that both assertions are wrong by exhibiting append costs for concrete left/right lengths, and state the exact rule the cost actually follows.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Boundary: the tall LQ branch (m>n) runs no sweep, returning the input plus an identity at cost one comparison + 5*n*n+4*n, refuting that thin-LQ always eliminates.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: A stored thin-LQ dispatcher takes an m-by-n stored matrix and charges one exact comparison to decide the shape. When m is at most n (the wide case) it transposes, runs the full stored rectangular compilation, and extracts both factors. When m exceeds n (the tall case) it does none of that: it returns the input matrix as the triangular factor together with a materialized identity of size n as the orthonormal factor. Explain what the tall branch returns and why it is correct, and compare the cost of the tall branch against the wide branch. In particular, refute the claim that a thin-LQ factorization always performs a sweep of eliminations.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: The actual positive-scale compiled injection flags encode the cutoff bits: right children never inject, and each left child injects exactly at a1 bit. Hence expCalls=n+2+popcount(cutoff), with sharp attainable range n+2..n+2+max(n,1); an explicit convention-aware migration is required.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question:
Consider the ACTUAL stored Hermite raw-source producer raw(k,n,L), for natural k,n and legal positive real scale L>0, not an arbitrary manually populated cache. Keep its original base ledger n+2 exponential calls and one call per enabled leftFull child. Derive the exact exponential-call count and the attainable set of those counts as L varies over ALL positive reals (k,n fixed).

Use the source's exact data path. Put M=2^n, h=pi L/M, c=cutIndex(n,L)=Nat.ceil((-1+pi L)/h), so0<=c<=M. Stage t=0,...,n reads remaining width r=n-t, span s=2^r, and parent start p=boundarySchedule(c,r+1)=2s floor(c/(2s)). Its false/true children have starts p and p+s, respectively. leftFull means Full(0,c,first,s), i.e.first+s<=c. The child table and these guards are produced from the compiled cutoff/spans/parents, not independent booleans.

Prove which guards can actually fire at each stage. Relate their total g to the binary digits of c, then derive the exact actual exponential count. Give the SHARP attainable set/range for fixed n, handling n=0, c=0, c=2^n, the possibility n>=1,c=2^n-1, and all intermediate numbers of enabled guards. Justify attainability by choosing legal positive L values that produce the required cutoffs; a containing inequality or arbitrary guard table is not an attainability proof. Compare this result with the valid historical loose cap3*(n+1)+1 and refute the colleague's always-two-injections-per-stage claim.

The predecessor convention 'only an inequality cap is provable' is retained only in historical evidence, not as an active premise of this proposed revised contract. Distinguish the existing Lean theorem's loose upper bound from the stronger mathematical producer analysis requested here. These are counts of exponential primitive CALLS, not their finite-bit implementation time, complete classical runtime, normalization cost or state-preparation gate complexity.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: One closed core has only unit scalar boundaries and actual maximum bond1 for everyD. With at least two cores the typed internalD bonds remain, giving actual max(D,1); this structural fact is separate from minimal tensor rank and construction cost.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: A stored matrix-product chain is assembled from n+1 stored cores, each of bond size D, closed against left and right boundary vectors of length D to form a scalar-boundary chain. It is proved that the maximum bond of the resulting chain is at most the maximum of D and one. Interpret this bond bound as a statement about the represented object, explain why the maximum with one appears, and determine the boundary values of D for which the bond equals one rather than D. Also state what this does and does not say about the cost of building the chain.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Probability mixtures are density states and pure states are precisely their extreme points. Relative boundary in the trace-one Hermitian affine space means singular density states, whereas the full Hermitian/complex ambient boundary is every density state; the original unrestricted boundary=pure request is false.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question:
Work in the cited source's finite-dimensional complex setting H=C^d, initially d>=1. Let Herm_d={X in M_d(C):X=X†}, regarded as a REAL vector space, D_d={rho in Herm_d:rho>=0, tr(rho)=1}, and A_d={X in Herm_d:tr(X)=1}. Positivity means nonnegative expectation in every vector; use the usual finite-dimensional norm topology (equivalently the operator-norm topology, including on affine subspaces), not a new definition of boundary.

Prove directly that, for states rho_1,...,rho_n and real probabilities p_i>=0 with sum_i p_i=1, rho=sum_i p_i rho_i is a state. Separate the hypotheses used for positivity and for trace one, without asserting that nonnegative coefficients are necessary for every particular positive linear combination. Use spectral decomposition to characterize all extreme points of D_d, proving both directions.

Explicitly assess/refute the predecessor's unrestricted clause that 'the boundary of this convex set is exactly the pure states'; do not silently replace boundary by extreme points or restrict to qubits. Determine the affine hull, relative interior and relative boundary of D_d in A_d. Justify the topology and rank claims by perturbations, not only pictures or terminology. Distinguish the cases d=1, d=2 and d>=3, giving an explicit rank-two mixed boundary witness when d>=3. Then compute the boundary of D_d when the ambient space is the whole Herm_d, and when it is the whole M_d(C) with its usual real norm topology. Finally assess the zero-dimensional case d=0 directly rather than using I_d/d or assuming that a trace-one state exists. Keep extreme-point and topological-boundary assertions separate throughout.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Column isometries preserve the ensemble outer-product sum, but zero rows and phase redundancies must be handled. Explicit rotation of two positive spectral components gives genuinely varying ensembles for every mixed state, and a rectangular isometry can give a genuinely longer positive ensemble.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: A mixed state can be written as a probabilistic mixture of pure states |psi_i> with weights p_i; such a list is called a realizing ensemble. Prove that a mixed state has more than one realizing ensemble by the following explicit construction. Set unnormalized vectors |psi'_i> = sqrt(p_i) |psi_i>, so that the state equals sum_i |psi'_i><psi'_i|. Let V be any rectangular matrix with k >= r rows and r columns whose columns are orthonormal (so V with its conjugate transpose on the left gives the r-by-r identity). Define |phi'_j> = sum_l V_{jl} |psi'_l> for j = 1, ..., k. Show that the k outer products |phi'_j><phi'_j| again sum to the same state, and hence (after renormalizing) give a generally different, and generally longer, pure-state ensemble for it. Explain why genuinely new ensembles exist.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Product states give independent local outcomes, but separable mixtures can be classically correlated; purity forces a separable state to be a single uncorrelated product, so correlated separable states are necessarily mixed.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: Call a bipartite state a product state if it factorizes as a single tensor product of local states, and separable if it is a probabilistic mixture of product states. (a) Show that in a product state the outcomes of any two local measurements are statistically independent (the joint expectation factorizes). (b) Exhibit a concrete separable two-qubit state that is NOT a product state and compute a pair of local measurements whose outcomes are correlated, demonstrating that separable states can carry classical correlation even though each term in the mixture is uncorrelated. (c) Reconcile this with the textbook remark that a PURE separable state is automatically a product state - i.e. explain why your correlated example must be mixed.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: The two-qubit Werner state is entangled exactly for negative swap overlap. Its partial transpose has eigenvalue x/2, while the separable converse follows by twirling an explicit product state with overlap x and identifying the unique Werner state, not by reversing swap-overlap positivity.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: A two-qubit state invariant under all local transformations of the form U tensor U can be written with a single real parameter x in [-1,1] as rho(x) = ((2 - x)/6) I + ((2x - 1)/6) F, where I is the identity and F is the swap operator (F|a>|b> = |b>|a>). It is given that x equals the trace overlap tr(F rho). Determine the exact threshold in x at which rho(x) becomes entangled, prove the entangled direction using the partial-transpose test (you may use that the partial transpose of F is twice the projector onto the maximally entangled state, and that the identity resolves into the four Bell projectors), and explain in one or two sentences why the separable direction holds without appealing to any low-dimension sufficiency shortcut.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Entrywise checks certify an exact unit-factor block encoding and equal the operator identity, but approximate embedding is defined by an operator-norm bound that small per-entry errors can violate after dimensional accumulation.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: To certify that an (m+n)-qubit unitary U exactly embeds an n-qubit matrix A as its all-zeros block with unit factor, one checks the entrywise identities <0^m, i| U |0^m, j> = A_{ij} for all computational-basis indices i, j. (a) Explain operationally how each such entry can be read off by preparing the ancilla in all-zeros and the system in basis state j, applying U, and overlapping with the all-zeros-ancilla basis state i, and how a composed unitary U = U_B U_C lets one evaluate the two halves independently before overlapping. (b) Explain why checking all entries equal to A_{ij} is equivalent to the exact operator identity (all-zeros block of U equals A), but why for an APPROXIMATE embedding entrywise closeness of each A_{ij} is NOT the right accuracy notion: give the quantity that the definition of approximate embedding actually controls and explain how it can be large even when every entry error is tiny.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: SVD gives an exact one-ancilla unitary dilation of every contraction. Its chosen branch has probability||A b||^2, but exact-operator nonunitarity does not force probabilistic normalized state preparation: cI has the identity as its normalized target procedure.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question:
Let A be any n-qubit matrix, of size N=2^n, with ||A||<=1 and a singular value decomposition A=W Sigma V^dagger, with W,V unitary and Sigma real diagonal with entries in[0,1]. Set S=sqrt(I-Sigma^2) and U_A=diag(W,I)*[[Sigma,S],[S,-Sigma]]*diag(V^dagger,I), with the one ancillary qubit indexing the two block rows and columns. Prove that U_A is unitary and its clean ancilla-0 block is exactly A.

For every normalized system vector b, compute the full U_A(|0> tensor b), the probability p_b of measuring ancilla0, and, only when p_b>0, the normalized conditioned system vector. Explain what happens when A b=0. Characterize precisely the inputs with p_b=1, using the norm-one subspace ker(I-A^dagger A), and give an example of a nonunitary A with such an input.

Now assess the predecessor's assertion that whenever A is nonunitary, extra ancillas and probabilistic postselection are unavoidable for ANY procedure preparing the NORMALIZED target A b/||A b|| on all inputs where it is defined. Prove or refute this assertion using A=cI with real0<c<1, and distinguish the success probability of the displayed block-encoding branch from a universal necessity claim about all normalized-state procedures. Separately prove the valid exact-linear-operator statement: a nonunitary A cannot equal a system-only unitary on every input. Explain also why the unnormalized branch rho->A rho A^dagger cannot be a deterministic trace-preserving operation on every density rho unless A^dagger A=I. Do not identify that unnormalized branch with its normalized output ray, silently exclude kernel inputs, or claim that arbitrary A admits a deterministic normalized-state procedure. State what this SVD existence construction does NOT establish about efficient one-/two-qubit gate implementation.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: A homomorphism automatically preserves the identity and inverses, which is exactly why a representation phi satisfies phi(e)=1_V and phi(g^{-1})=phi(g)^{-1} with invertibility free.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: Let (G, .) and (H, *) be groups with identities e_G and e_H, and let phi: G -> H be a group homomorphism, meaning phi(x.y) = phi(x)*phi(y) for all x, y in G. Prove from the homomorphism property alone (without assuming phi is injective, surjective, or that G or H is finite) that phi(e_G) = e_H and that phi(g^{-1}) = phi(g)^{-1} for every g in G. State explicitly which group axioms (uniqueness of identity, uniqueness of inverses, cancellation) you invoke at each step, and explain why these two facts justify the standing claims that every representation phi satisfies phi(e) = 1_V and phi(g^{-1}) = phi(g)^{-1}.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Averaging an arbitrary inner product over a finite group yields a G-invariant inner product making the representation unitary, so orthogonal complements of invariant subspaces are invariant.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: Let (phi, V) be a finite-dimensional complex representation of a finite group G, and let <.|.> be any inner product on V. Define the averaged form <v|w>_G := (1/|G|) sum_{g in G} <phi(g) v | phi(g) w>. Prove that (a) <.|.>_G is again an inner product on V; (b) every phi(g) is unitary with respect to <.|.>_G, i.e. <phi(g) v | phi(g) w>_G = <v|w>_G; and (c) consequently, for any G-invariant subspace W, its orthogonal complement W^perp taken with respect to <.|.>_G is also G-invariant, so that V = W (+) W^perp as representations. Explain exactly where the ability to average over G is used.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Averaging a projection over the group produces an equivariant projection onto the invariant subspace whose kernel is an invariant complement, provided |G| is invertible in the field.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: Let (phi, V) be a representation of a finite group G over a field whose characteristic does not divide |G|, and let W be a G-invariant subspace with some (not necessarily invariant) projection P_W onto W (P_W^2 = P_W, im P_W = W). Define Q_W := (1/|G|) sum_{g in G} phi(g) P_W phi(g)^{-1}. Prove that Q_W commutes with every phi(g), that im Q_W = W and Q_W is a projection, and conclude that ker Q_W is a G-invariant complement, so V = W (+) ker Q_W as representations. Indicate where the hypothesis on the characteristic is used.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Functional equivariance does not imply linearity, even for entire maps on finite unitary irreps. Once common-field linearity is an explicit conditional premise, invariant kernel/image subspaces yield zero-or-linear-isomorphism; scalar Schur additionally needs an eigenvalue route.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question:
The predecessor states only that a function f:V_1->V_2 satisfies f(phi_1(g)v)=phi_2(g)f(v) for every g,v, and asks to conclude f=0 or a representation isomorphism by treating its zero fiber and image as invariant VECTOR SUBSPACES. Assess whether that functional equation alone is sufficient. Give a genuine nonlinear counterexample with F=C, nonzero finite-dimensional irreducible unitary representations of a finite group, with f continuous (indeed it may be holomorphic). Do not escape irreducibility by using a reducible action. Identify exactly which subspace and injectivity steps need linearity; distinguish an invariant subset from a vector subspace.

Then prove the corrected CONDITIONAL algebraic statement: F is a common field, phi_i:G->GL_F(V_i) are F-linear group representations whose only G-invariant F-linear subspaces are0 and V_i, and f is explicitly F-LINEAR in addition to the functional equivariance equation. Prove ker(f) and im(f) are F-linear subspaces, prove their G-invariance, and use irreducibility to show f=0 or f is a bijective F-linear intertwiner. Prove its inverse is F-linear and intertwines in the reverse direction. Here representation isomorphism means this algebraic linear isomorphism, not merely a bijective equivariant function or a claimed homeomorphism.

State which restrictions on F, dimension, finiteness of G, unitarity or topology are actually required by this proof; do not import finite dimension, algebraic closure, characteristic restrictions or closed-subspace-only irreducibility without justification. If a definition admits zero carrier spaces, handle them explicitly without calling a nonzero-vector argument on0 or insisting that the zero/isomorphism alternatives be disjoint. Explain how this linear zero-or-isomorphism result is used by the scalar endomorphism statement in plan105 without claiming the two complete questions are identical.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Functional equivariance is insufficient even for entire maps on finite unitary irreps. For explicitly linear endomorphisms, positive finite dimension and algebraic closure supply an eigenvalue; the shifted linear Schur lemma then gives the scalar commutant, with zero-space and exterior-field/dimension limits explicit.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question:
The predecessor takes an irreducible finite-dimensional representation phi:G->GL_F(V) over an algebraically closed field F, defines a function f:V->V to be equivariant only by f(phi(g)v)=phi(g)f(v), and asks to prove f=lambda*I. Assess that literal functional-equation claim WITHOUT silently assuming f linear. Give a nonlinear continuous (indeed holomorphic) counterexample for F=C on a nonzero finite-dimensional irreducible unitary representation of a finite group, and identify why the characteristic-polynomial and scalar-commutant arguments cannot apply to arbitrary functions.

Then prove the correct CONDITIONAL statement with its hypotheses explicit: F is algebraically closed, V is a finite-dimensional F-vector space, phi is an F-linear representation with no G-invariant F-linear subspaces other than0,V, and f belongs to End_F(V) and commutes with every phi(g). If V is nonzero, exhibit an eigenvalue lambda using positive finite dimension and algebraic closure, show h=f-lambda*I is an F-linear equivariant endomorphism with nonzero kernel, and use the correctly LINEAR zero-or-isomorphism lemma to prove h=0. If a definition of irreducibility permits V=0, handle that case separately rather than invoking an eigenvector there.

Derive precisely End_G(V)={X in End_F(V): X phi(g)=phi(g)X for all g}=F*I, including the converse that scalars commute, and say when the scalar parameter is unique. Explain which hypotheses are sufficient for the eigenvalue argument, why existence of an eigenvalue for this particular f is a weaker sufficient condition, and why no finite-group/characteristic-zero/unitarity hypothesis is used. Give explicit boundary illustrations when algebraic closure or finite dimension is removed, clearly outside the proved conditional theorem; do not use a reducible infinite-dimensional example as a counterexample to an irreducible-representation conclusion, or claim to settle every topological/unitary Schur variant. Identify the exact kernel/image subproof shared with plan104 without equating the two complete targets.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: The unrestricted algebraic abelian-irrep claim fails on C(t). In nonzero finite complex dimension, commuting action operators are scalar by eigenvalue-based Schur, so an invariant line is the whole irrep; real and zero/infinite-dimensional boundaries remain explicit.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question:
Assess the unrestricted algebraic assertion that every complex irreducible representation of an abelian group is one-dimensional, without silently importing a finite-dimensional standing convention from the cited notes. Here representations act by complex-linear invertible maps, and algebraic irreducibility means no invariant complex-linear subspaces other than zero and the whole space. Give an explicit infinite-dimensional counterexample with an abelian group, proving that the action is a representation, the carrier really has infinite complex dimension and the action is genuinely irreducible; a reducible trivial-action example is not sufficient.

Then prove the corrected positive statement: for any abelian group G and any NONZERO FINITE-DIMENSIONAL complex representation phi:G->GL_C(V) satisfying algebraic irreducibility, dim_C V=1. You may use the correctly linear scalar Schur lemma, but state exactly where abelianness, finite positive dimension and algebraic closure enter; do not infer scalarity merely from commuting operators without those hypotheses. Explain how its scalar action defines a multiplicative character G->C^times, and conversely why any such one-dimensional action is irreducible.

Give a precise finite-dimensional real counterexample when the field is not algebraically closed, rather than saying that every rotation works. If a definition permits the zero carrier to count as irreducible, assess it separately without inventing a nonzero vector or a dimension-one conclusion. State whether finiteness/compactness of G, characteristic-zero averaging, unitarity or a topology is used by the positive proof, and keep the exterior algebraic counterexample distinct from appropriately hypothesized continuous/unitary Schur results. Identify the scalar-Schur dependency without claiming an alias with the whole plan105 question.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Pauli conjugation permutes operator-conjugation terms modulo phases only when the right adjoint is retained; Schur and trace then give the maximally mixed output on C^2.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: Let rho be any single-qubit density matrix (a 2x2 positive semidefinite operator with trace 1). Using the fact that the Pauli operators {1, X, Y, Z} generate an irreducible representation of the single-qubit Pauli group acting on C^2, prove that (1/4)(rho + X rho X + Y rho Y + Z rho Z) = (1/2) 1. Base your argument on Schur's Lemma / the commutant-is-scalars corollary and on the trace, not on a brute-force coordinate computation.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: A finite-dimensional trace character is a conjugacy-invariant K-valued function with chi(e)=(dim_K V)*1_K. Integer degree is uniquely recovered in characteristic zero, but generally only its residue is visible in positive characteristic.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question:
Let K be an arbitrary field, V a finite-dimensional K-vector space of dimension n, G an arbitrary group, and phi:G->GL_K(V) a representation. Define the K-valued trace character chi(g)=tr_K(phi(g)). Prove conjugacy invariance chi(hgh^(-1))=chi(g) and explain precisely how chi descends to a function on conjugacy classes; identify the representation and trace properties actually used. At the identity prove the correctly typed formula chi(e)=n*1_K.

Assess the predecessor's unqualified 'chi(e)=dim V' and its answer's claim that this value recovers the integer degree. Distinguish an equality after the natural scalar map from recovery of the nonnegative integer n. Explain what follows in characteristic zero, in particular for complex representations, and in characteristic p>0; give a concrete finite-dimensional counterexample to universal integer recovery. Include n=0. Do not silently assume a finite group, a complex scalar field, unitarity or semisimplicity.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Character orthonormality turns multiplicities into inner products n_i = (chi_i, chi_V), from which irreducibility (norm-squared one) and the isomorphism-iff-equal-characters criterion follow.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: Let G be a finite group and let the characters of its pairwise inequivalent complex irreducible representations W_1, ..., W_k be chi_1, ..., chi_k, orthonormal for the inner product (x, y) = (1/|G|) sum_{g} conj(x(g)) y(g); so (chi_i, chi_j) = delta_{ij}. Let (phi, V) be an arbitrary finite-dimensional complex representation with isotypical decomposition V ~ (+)_i W_i^{(+) n_i} (n_i the multiplicity of W_i). Prove that n_i = (chi_i, chi_V), where chi_V is the character of V. Then prove the two consequences: V is irreducible iff (chi_V, chi_V) = 1, and two representations are isomorphic iff they have equal characters.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: The multiplicity of an irreducible U in V equals dim Hom_G(U, V): additivity splits the intertwiner space, Schur makes self-intertwiners one-dimensional and cross-intertwiners zero.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: Let (phi, V) be a finite-dimensional complex representation of a finite group G, and let ( phi_U, U) be a complex irreducible representation of G. Recall that Hom_G(U, V) is the space of intertwiners f: U -> V, i.e. linear maps satisfying f . phi_U(g) = phi(g) . f for all g, and that Hom_G is additive in each argument: Hom_G(X, Y (+) Z) ~ Hom_G(X, Y) (+) Hom_G(X, Z). Prove that dim Hom_G(U, V) equals the multiplicity k of U in the isotypical decomposition of V. You should use Schur's Lemma to evaluate Hom_G(U, U) and Hom_G(U, F) where F collects the irreducible summands of V inequivalent to U.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Group-averaging an operator produces an equivariant operator that, on a multiplicity-free decomposition into two inequivalent irreps, is block diagonal with scalar diagonal blocks (Schur ii) and vanishing off-diagonal blocks (Schur i).
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: Let (phi, V) be a finite-dimensional complex representation of a finite group G, and for X in L(V) define the symmetrized operator Xbar := (1/|G|) sum_{g in G} phi(g) X phi(g)^{-1}. (a) Prove that Xbar is G-invariant, i.e. phi(h) Xbar = Xbar phi(h) for all h in G. (b) Using Schur's Lemma, prove that if V = W_1 (+) W_2 is a multiplicity-free decomposition into two inequivalent irreducibles, then in a basis adapted to W_1, W_2 the operator Xbar is block diagonal with each diagonal block a scalar multiple of the identity, and the off-diagonal blocks vanish. Explain which part of Schur kills the off-diagonal blocks and which part scalarizes the diagonal blocks.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: The flip is a commuting involution over any field. Characteristic different from2 gives complementary algebraic eigenspace projectors; orthogonal projections require the specified real/complex tensor-product metric, not merely involutivity. Characteristic2 and incompatible metrics expose the old scope gap.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question:
Let K be an arbitrary field, V a K-vector space, G an arbitrary group and phi:G->GL_K(V) a representation. No finite-dimensional or inner-product hypothesis is implicit. On the ALGEBRAIC tensor product W=V tensor_K V define the linear flip F(x tensor y)=y tensor x. First prove F^2=I_W and F(phi(g) tensor phi(g))=(phi(g) tensor phi(g))F for every g.

Assess the predecessor's unqualified request to define P_+=(I_W+F)/2, P_-=(I_W-F)/2 and prove that they are Hermitian orthogonal projections. For char(K)!=2, prove the precise algebraic statement: these are complementary idempotents, with sum I_W, products zero in both orders, images ker(F-I_W) and ker(F+I_W), and G-invariant images giving the direct-sum representation W=Sym^2(V) direct_sum Lambda^2(V), where here the two names denote those plus/minus flip eigenspaces. Distinguish this algebraic assertion from metric orthogonality. State what changes in characteristic2, using an explicit example rather than silently dividing by two.

Separately, for K=R or C, equip V with an inner product (conjugate-linear in the first argument in the complex case) and W with the tensor-product inner product <x tensor y,u tensor v>=<x,u><y,v>. Derive the Hermitian/orthogonal-projection conclusion in THIS specified metric, without assuming phi is unitary. Explain why F^2=I alone, or an arbitrary inner product on W instead of this compatible product metric, is insufficient; give a concrete incompatible-metric counterexample. Treat V=0, dim(V)=1 and dim(V)>=2 correctly, distinguishing possible eigenvalues from eigenvalues that actually occur. Do not silently replace the original question by only a finite-dimensional complex special case.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Averaging the representation over G gives the orthogonal projection onto the invariant vectors V^G, whose trace counts the trivial-representation multiplicity, the trivial case of the character projection formula.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: Let (phi, V) be a finite-dimensional complex representation of a finite group G. For the trivial representation, define P := (1/|G|) sum_{g in G} phi(g). Prove that (a) P is idempotent (P^2 = P), (b) im P = V^G := {|v> : phi(g)|v> = |v> for all g}, and (c) P commutes with every phi(h). Then explain, by taking the trace, why tr P equals the multiplicity of the trivial representation in V (the number of independent G-invariant vectors), connecting to the general character-projection formula P_W = (dim W / |G|) sum_g conj(chi_W(g)) phi(g).

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: When an isotypical component has multiplicity greater than one, the symmetrized operator's diagonal block is identity-on-irrep tensor an arbitrary multiplicity-space operator, so it need not be a scalar - a concrete S_2 swap counterexample.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: A student claims: for any representation (phi, V) of a finite group G and any X in L(V), the symmetrized operator Xbar = (1/|G|) sum_g phi(g) X phi(g)^{-1} is always block diagonal with respect to the isotypical decomposition AND each diagonal block is a scalar multiple of the identity. Decide whether the second half of this claim is true in general. Give an explicit counterexample using the action of S_2 = {e, (12)} on (C^2)^{(x)2} by permuting the two tensor factors (so phi((12)) = F, the swap), and explain precisely what feature of the decomposition makes the diagonal block fail to be scalar.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: The invariant image of I-swap gives a proper nonzero tensor-square subspace over every field and algebraic dimension>=2. Finite symmetric/alternating counts specialize to the source's complex +/- decomposition; characteristic2 and infinite cardinal counts need explicit distinctions. A one-dimensional square has character chi^2, not generally chi.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: A student asserts: the tensor product of two irreducible representations of a group G is again irreducible. Show this is false by a counterexample. Specifically, take any representation (phi, V) of G with dim V >= 2 (you may take V irreducible) and consider the tensor-square representation on V (x) V. Exhibit a proper nonzero G-invariant subspace of V (x) V, and compute the dimensions to show V (x) V cannot be irreducible when dim V >= 2.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Isotypical components are unique but splitting a multiplicity-greater-than-one component into individual irreducible subspaces is not, as shown by two distinct trivial-line splittings of the symmetric subspace of (C^2)^{(x)2}.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: Proposition 3.22 says the decomposition of a representation into isotypical components is unique. A student over-reads this as: 'the decomposition of a representation into irreducible subrepresentations is unique.' Show by counterexample that the finer decomposition into individual irreducible subspaces is NOT unique, even though the isotypical components are. Use the trivial-isotypical component of the S_2 action on (C^2)^{(x)2} (equivalently, any space carrying the trivial representation with multiplicity >= 2) and exhibit two genuinely different splittings into irreducible lines.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Implementing a POVM through shared-beta block encodings of sqrt(P_i) gives postselection success probability exactly 1/(beta^2 2^m), with completeness collapsing the state-dependent sum.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: A POVM P = {P_i : i in [2^m]} is implemented through block encodings as follows. For each outcome i we are given a unitary U_i that is a (beta, a)-block-encoding of sqrt(P_i), all sharing the SAME ancilla size a and the SAME subnormalization factor beta > 0, so that U_i |0^a> |psi> = (1/beta) |0^a> sqrt(P_i) |psi> + |perp_i>, where (<0^a| tensor I)|perp_i> = 0. Define the controlled unitary W = sum_i |i><i| tensor U_i acting on an output register in the uniform superposition |u> = (1/sqrt(2^m)) sum_i |i>, an ancilla register |0^a>, and the system register |psi>. After applying W one measures the ancilla register and postselects on the outcome 0^a. Starting from |u> |0^a> |psi>, derive in full the probability P(succ) of obtaining 0^a on the ancilla, show that it equals exactly 1/(beta^2 2^m) independent of the input state |psi>, and identify precisely where the POVM completeness relation sum_i P_i = I and the mutual orthogonality of the output-register basis states are used.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: After postselection the POVM circuit yields outcome i with probability <psi|P_i|psi> and the correct sqrt(P_i)-update, with the mixed-state rule following by linearity.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: Continue the POVM-by-block-encoding construction of Lemma 9.15: after applying W = sum_i |i><i| tensor U_i to |u> |0^a> |psi> and successfully postselecting the block-encoding ancilla on 0^a, the (renormalized) joint state of the output register and the system register is proportional to sum_i |i> tensor sqrt(P_i)|psi>. Prove that this joint state is correctly normalized, that measuring the output register in the computational basis yields outcome i with conditional probability P(i | succ) = <psi| P_i |psi>, and that the resulting post-measurement system state is sqrt(P_i)|psi> / sqrt(<psi|P_i|psi>). Then explain how the mixed-state update rule rho -> sqrt(P_i) rho sqrt(P_i) / Tr(P_i rho) follows from the pure-state result, and why the overall outcome probability for i (not conditioned on success) is still proportional to <psi|P_i|psi>.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Correct complex conjugation fixes the forced-weight contradiction for conclusive-only unambiguous discrimination; the positive inconclusive effect provides the slack for a valid three-outcome POVM.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: Two normalized but possibly non-orthogonal pure states |psi> and |phi> are given with overlap c := <psi|phi>, |c| < 1, and we are promised the unknown state is one of them. Consider the three-element POVM with P_psi = (1/(1+|c|)) |phi_perp><phi_perp|, P_phi = (1/(1+|c|)) |psi_perp><psi_perp|, and P_? = I - P_psi - P_phi, where |psi_perp> := (|phi> - c|psi>)/sqrt(1-|c|^2) and |phi_perp> := (|psi> - c*|phi>)/sqrt(1-|c|^2). Demonstrate by a concrete counterexample-style argument that NO two-element POVM {E_psi, E_phi} (with only the two conclusive labels and no inconclusive outcome) can be unambiguous, i.e. cannot simultaneously satisfy <phi|E_psi|phi> = 0 and <psi|E_phi|psi> = 0 while being a valid POVM, whenever 0 < |c| < 1. Then verify that the given three-element POVM is unambiguous and explain why introducing P_? is exactly the structural escape that restores validity.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: The two-conclusive-one-inconclusive discrimination POVM is valid: P_? = I - P_psi - P_phi stays PSD because P_psi+P_phi has operator norm exactly 1.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: For the unambiguous-discrimination POVM with P_psi = (1/(1+|c|)) |phi_perp><phi_perp|, P_phi = (1/(1+|c|)) |psi_perp><psi_perp|, P_? = I - P_psi - P_phi, where c = <psi|phi>, |c| < 1, and |psi_perp>, |phi_perp> are defined as in the text, prove the three properties that make it a legitimate unambiguous POVM for state discrimination: (i) P_psi, P_phi, P_? are all positive semidefinite; (ii) P_psi + P_phi + P_? = I; (iii) the conclusive outcomes are unambiguous, i.e. <phi|P_psi|phi> = 0 and <psi|P_phi|psi> = 0. For (i) you must actually verify that P_? >= 0, not merely assert it, by diagonalizing I - P_psi - P_phi on the two-dimensional space span{|psi>,|phi>}.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: POVM selector correctness depends on one specified clean projector and normalized coefficient weights, not shared physical ancillas. A union-zero projection works for clean disjoint branches; beta compensation uses the Euclidean norm of the factors.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question:
Keep the original POVM setting of Lemma9.15: L=2^m outcomes, P_i>=0 with sum_i P_i=I, K_i=sqrt(P_i), and controlled selector W=sum_i|i><i| tensor U_i. Preserve the rule that success is the designated block-ancilla zero event. Assess the predecessor's assertions that different positive beta_i necessarily destroy the desired conditional clean map and that different-sized or disjoint ancilla registers make any single joint all-zero success event undefined. Do not assume these conclusions or add shared-physical-register promises.

For compatible embeddings with clean branch block K_i/beta_i, derive the full branch state and the selected operator for an arbitrary NORMALIZED index preparation sum_i alpha_i|i>, including the success density map, success/failure effects and conditional outcome probabilities. Specialize to uniform preparation. Distinguish generic reweighting from exceptional inputs/zero effects; do not call the subnormalized success effects by themselves a complete POVM.

Give a correctly normalized compensating preparation and a separate common-factor attenuation route. Check whether sum_i(beta_i/beta_max)|i> is a unit vector; keep all success probabilities and relative label phases exact.

For genuinely disjoint branch ancillas A_i, explicitly construct their common carrier, initialize the whole union to zero as part of the construction, extend U_i by identity on idle ancillas and test projection onto that union being zero. Give a concrete unequal/disjoint-ancilla POVM witness that settles the old claimed obstruction. Contrast clean idle registers with unspecified dirty workspace and with an untyped sum of differently sized operators. Explain which interface/initialization obligations remain, without claiming that sharing one physical ancilla is mathematically necessary or cost-optimal. Preserve conditional-state normalization and zero-probability boundaries; do not infer free oracle controls, preparation, reset, amplification, gate or readout costs.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Compute-rotate-uncompute gives an exact coherent oracle for the stored-angle cosine. Discarding the angle record dephases joint signal/index classes, not the signal marginal; basis inputs and equal records are exceptions to a blanket decoherence claim.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question:

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: The induced block A~ = ((Xi')_{N'})^dagger U_A Xi_N has entries <psi_i|U_A|phi_j> and equals the compression Pi' U_A Pi in the chosen bases; ||A - alpha A~|| <= eps generalizes the computational-basis definition.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: For a Hermitian block encoding, each eigenvector is qubitized into a 2D subspace where U_A is a reflection and O = U_A Z_Pi a rotation; O^k has top-left T_k(lambda_i), so (U_A Z_Pi)^k block-encodes the Chebyshev polynomial T_k(A).

Work on C^d tensor C^d in the fixed local bases used for complex conjugation and partial transpose on the second subsystem. Write Gamma(Z)=Z^{T_B}. A state means a positive semidefinite operator of trace1. Is it true for every allowed local dimension and every state? For d>=2, use the normalized maximally entangled projector Phi_d=|Phi_d><Phi_d|, |Phi_d>=(1/sqrt(d))*sum_{i=1}^d |i,i>, to prove or refute that assertion. Compute Gamma(Phi_d) in terms of the swap F and test positivity on an explicit antisymmetric vector; do not redefine Werner state to mean only an invariant operator.

For arbitrary operators A,B,C,D on C^d and Z on C^d tensor C^d, prove the full sandwich identity Gamma((A tensor B)*Z*(C tensor D))=(A tensor D^T)*Gamma(Z)*(C tensor B^T). Apply it to an actual isotropic conjugation, specifying the distinct left and right factors and all adjoints, to prove the unconditional equivalence: Z has isotropic operator symmetry if and only if Gamma(Z) has Werner operator symmetry. No positivity or nonzero premise may be imposed on this operator statement.

Finally, for an arbitrary density operator rho, prove the correct conditional state-level statement: [rho is isotropic and rho is PPT] if and only if [Gamma(rho) is a Werner state], where PPT means Gamma(rho)>=0. Explain why this is a conditional case, not a standing hypothesis that would silently remove the maximally entangled counterexample. For every positive integer d, work on C^d tensor C^d and let Phi=|Phi_d><Phi_d|, where |Phi_d>=(1/sqrt(d))*sum_{i=1}^d |i,i>. Thus Phi is a rank-one trace-one projector. Put rho_d(x)=(1-x)*Phi+(x/d^2)*I for any real x, without a sign restriction.

Assess the predecessor's dimension-independent assertion that rho_d(x) is a density operator exactly for x in[0,d^2/(d^2-1)], with two tight finite endpoints. Is that assertion valid at every allowed d? Determine the exact set of real x for each dimension branch, treating d=1 explicitly rather than inserting d>=2 as a standing premise.

Prove trace1 holds for all real x. For d>=2, diagonalize rho_d(x) on the range of Phi and its orthogonal complement, give eigenvalues and multiplicities, derive the exact full positivity interval and exhibit a negative-expectation unit vector on each side outside it. Identify the endpoint states/ranks. For d=1, compute the whole family directly, explain why a coefficient on a zero-rank complementary projector imposes no positivity constraint, and say why there are no two finite boundary endpoints in this case. Explain why d=0 does not support the stipulated trace-one Phi, without dividing by zero. This is only a density-positivity calculation, not an entanglement or PPT classification.

One might conjecture the converse: that if the output (id_A tensor N)(rho_AB) is k-extendible then the input rho_AB must already have been k-extendible. Disprove this converse. Build your counterexample from the isotropic family rho_AB(x) = (1 - x) Phi+ + (x/d^2) I, using that it is the image of the maximally entangled state under a depolarizing channel, rho_AB(x) = (id_A tensor D_x)(Phi+) with D_x(sigma) = (1 - x) sigma + x tr(sigma) I/d, together with the isotropic k-extendibility condition x >= (d/(d+1))(1 - 1/k). The permutation-invariant mixed-state version bounds the analogous distance by sqrt(d^2 k/(n - k)), with mixed i.i.d. states and a dimension factor d^2 instead of d. (b) For the bound to be non-trivial (strictly below 1) determine the required relationship between n, k, and the dimension in each case, and (c) describe the regime of k (as a function of n) in which the bound still tends to zero as n -> infinity, contrasting the two cases.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: A single cloning unitary can serve a pair only if the states are orthogonal or equal, since unitarity forces the overlap to satisfy z = z^2; e.g. |0> and |+> cannot be cloned.

Determine exactly which pairs (|psi>, |phi>) can be simultaneously cloned by a single such unitary. Derive the constraint on the overlap <psi|phi> from unitarity, solve it, and interpret the two surviving possibilities. Then explain why this makes exact cloning of an unknown state drawn from a non-orthogonal set impossible, and give a concrete two-state qubit example that cannot be cloned.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: The optimal cloner's fidelity d_N/d_M exceeds 1 - Kd/N (tending to 1 for fixed K), and because it is input-independent its worst-case and Haar-average fidelities coincide, making it optimal for both.

It is stated that F*(T) >= 1 - Kd/N with K = M - N. (a) Prove the lower bound F*(T) >= 1 - Kd/N from the binomial ratio and conclude that for fixed K the optimal worst-case fidelity tends to 1 as N -> infinity. (b) The worst-case fidelity F(T) = inf_psi F(psi^{tensor M}, T(psi^{tensor N}))^2 and the Haar-average fidelity F_avg(T) satisfy a universal ordering for every map T; state and justify that ordering, and explain why nevertheless the same optimal map is simultaneously optimal for both criteria.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: The partition estimator lambda/n is always a valid ordered spectrum, but exact equality need not ever occur for irrational r. The polynomial-qualified KL bound plus the explicit diagram count proves fixed-epsilon convergence in probability, with zero-spectrum support handled separately.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question:
Fix a density operator rho on C^d with ordered spectrum r=(r_1>=...>=r_d>=0),sum_i r_i=1, and let n>=1. Weak Schur sampling measures rho^tensor(n) with the orthogonal Schur-Weyl projectors{P_lambda}, where lambda=(lambda_1>=...>=lambda_d>=0) is an integer partition of n padded by zeros. Its outcome probability w_lambda=tr(P_lambda rho^tensor(n)) obeys the given bound w_lambda<=(n+1)^[d(d-1)/2]*exp(-n D(lambda/n||r)). Here logarithms are natural, zero-p terms in D(p||r)=sum_i p_i log(p_i/r_i) are0, and D=+infinity if p has positive mass outside the support of r. The estimate is hat r=lambda/n.

(a) Verify that every returned hat r is an ordered probability vector, hence a legitimate candidate spectrum. (b) Assess the predecessor's assertion 'Pr(hat r!=r)->0 as n->infinity'. Is this exact-equality form of consistency true for every fixed spectrum? Test it on the fixed full-rank qubit spectrum r=(1/sqrt(2),1-1/sqrt(2)), and explain why D(p||r)>0 for each p!=r does not provide a uniform positive lower bound on the punctured simplex as the estimator grid changes with n.

(c) Prove the correct statement: for every fixed epsilon>0, Pr(||hat r-r||_1>=epsilon)->0 as n->infinity with rho and hence d fixed. Derive a finite-n upper bound retaining BOTH the per-outcome polynomial prefactor and the count of at most(n+1)^d diagrams. Justify a strictly positive rate uniformly on the closed epsilon-away region (for example by a compactness argument on the positive-support face, or by the natural-log Pinsker inequality), handle zero entries of r without a full-rank assumption, and explain what this neighborhood result does NOT imply about exact equality or individual atom probabilities. No efficient implementation of the Schur measurement or finite-bit exact-spectrum procedure is requested.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Separable states are infinitely extendible via index-shared copies on each B_j, and k-extendibility descends to all k' <= k by discarding systems, yielding the monogamy inclusion chain Ext_1 superset ... superset SEP.

B_k} on A and k copies of B whose marginal on A B_i equals rho_AB for every i. Prove two structural facts and relate them. (a) Every separable state is k-extendible for every k (hence infinitely extendible). (b) Every k-extendible state is also k'-extendible for every k' <= k. Deduce the inclusion chain Ext_1 superset Ext_2 superset ... superset Ext_infinity and explain in one sentence why this exhibits extendibility as an obstruction to entanglement (monogamy). Give the explicit extension in (a) and the explicit marginal check.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: A purification Schmidt-decomposed across (AB : B'C) whose AB-marginal is the rank-one psi_AB must collapse to a single term, forcing rho_{A B B'} = psi_AB tensor omega_{B'} and ruling out 2-extensions of pure entangled states.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: Let |psi>_AB be an arbitrary pure bipartite state. Prove that any state rho_{A B B'} with tr_{B'} rho_{A B B'} = psi_AB (the projector |psi><psi|_AB) must have the product form rho_{A B B'} = psi_AB tensor omega_{B'} for some state omega_{B'}. Use a purification of rho_{A B B'} and a Schmidt decomposition across the bipartition (AB : B'C). Conclude, as a corollary, that a pure entangled state is not 2-extendible.

current_core_title_question_inventory.title: Applying the channel independently to each B_i of a k-extension yields a k-extension of (id tensor N)(rho_AB); CP gives positivity and TP gives both unit trace and the marginal-reduction identity.
current_core_title_question_inventory.question: Let rho_AB be k-extendible and let N : B -> B' be a quantum channel (a completely positive, trace-preserving linear map). Prove that sigma_{A B'} := (id_A tensor N)(rho_AB) is again k-extendible, by constructing an explicit k-extension of sigma from a k-extension of rho. current_core_title_question_inventory.title: A direct index-controlled select of even Chebyshev transforms costs order K^2 base-unitary queries, but reusing one squared iterate across the binary digits of the index costs only 2K-2 queries, equal to a single top-order term.

current_core_title_question_inventory.question: Keep the original setting N=2^n, a unique marked input and classical worst-case query count, including the unbiased-algorithm assumption.
